thesis: Human control needs resources and authority, not merely a position in a diagram.

ideas.statement: Calibrate trust by task and preserve practiced judgment and mentoring.
Decision density may increase fatigue even as routine work falls.

evidenceAndExamples.statement: There is a reassuring formulation: the human remains in the loop. But a place in a diagram does not guarantee the time, competence, and authority needed to control anything.

If someone approves hundreds of results they cannot examine, their presence can become ceremonial. If they answer for a decision without being able to see the evidence, responsibility is separated from power. If they can refuse only at the cost of missing an unrealistic deadline, approval is no longer simply a sign of confidence.

In a survey presented at CHI 2025, Lee and colleagues analyzed responses from 319 workers and 936 use examples. Greater trust in AI was associated with less reported critical effort, while critical activity shifted toward verification, integration, and task coordination. The study measures reported perceptions and practices; it does not demonstrate falling IQ or irreversible deterioration in the ability to think. [27]

Nor is reduced effort automatically bad. We do not want to mentally recalculate every result from a pocket calculator. The problem is calibration: do we save effort where the mechanism and context justify trust, or precisely where we lack the means to evaluate?

In Andrei’s fictional scenario, the agent solves ten simple problems well. The eleventh involves authorization and concurrency. Automatically transferring trust from the first ten to the last can be mistaken. “It worked before” is relevant information only if we understand exactly what is similar.

Delegation can free resources for more advanced thinking. But it can also eliminate opportunities to learn. The question is not whether using AI “makes us stupid” in general, but what operations we continue to practice and what operations become inaccessible when the tool is absent or wrong.

A junior who receives the complete solution can finish the task quickly without forming the mental model needed for the next one. Another junior can use the same system as a tutor: predict the result, receive a hint, explain why the test fails, reconstruct the solution. These are different educational scenarios, not inevitable effects of the same technology.

Teams can preserve code-reading exercises without generation, discussions of error causes, and reviews where the author must explain important properties. Not to protect typing as a ritual, but to preserve judgment. We need not know how to produce every component manually to use it; we must know enough for the responsibility we assume.

In a March 2026 interview, Matthew Kropp discusses survey findings on the overload people feel when using and supervising multiple AI tools. The expression “brain fry” is descriptive, not a diagnosis or evidence of brain injury. Such a report does not establish a universal number of agents a person can supervise. [44]

The practical explanation worth testing concerns decision density. If we automate repetitive parts and leave humans only the difficult exceptions, an hour may contain fewer routine movements and more consequential judgments. The activity can become more interesting and more tiring simultaneously.

We do not propose artificially reintroducing useless work. We propose recognizing that human time is not homogeneous. An hour of critical monitoring is not equivalent to an hour of familiar operations. A plan that counts only minutes can miss the difference in workload.

If every beginner’s question goes to a chatbot, the team may gain quiet. But it may also lose opportunities to discover what new members do not understand. Mentoring conveys more than an answer; it can convey criteria, the history of decisions, and how a problem is recognized.

This is an organizational hypothesis to be measured, not a condemnation of automated help. One solution might combine quick tutoring with periodic discussions of difficult cases. AI prepares the ground; people jointly build the criteria that have not yet been written.

The human left in control must be more than the final obstacle between generation and delivery. They must have a precise function, a manageable volume of work, and a real right to say the evidence is insufficient. Otherwise, “human control” can become a polite name for responsibility without resources.
PART V How to Build a Verification Machine

objectionsAndQualifications.statement: Survey is not IQ decline; brain fry is not diagnosis; hypotheses require measurement.

audit.notes: Complete chapter read; preserve proposed concepts, empirical limits and non-diagnostic distinctions.
